title: To develop an AI/ML-enabled adaptive noise cancellation (ANC) system that effectively suppresses stationary, non-stationary, and impulsive defence noises while maintaining high speech intelligibility and real-time performance on embedded hardware.
description:
• Background:
In defence and mission-critical communication systems, reliable speech transmission is severely affected by diverse acoustic disturbances such as gunshots, artillery fire, helicopter rotor noise, armored vehicle sound and emergency sirens. Traditional signal processing techniques-like spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, and classical LMS-based ANC-are limited in handling highly dynamic and non-linear noise environments. These methods assume stationary noise characteristics and often introduce artifacts or speech distortion under rapidly changing conditions.
Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML)
have transformed the field of speech enhancement and ANC. Deep learning models and time-domain architectures are capable of learning complex spectral-temporal patterns directly from data. These models significantly outperform conventional approaches in terms of perceptual quality (PESQ), intelligibility (STOI), and noise suppression (SNR). Additionally, the rise of edge AI platforms enables deployment of such models on embedded systems for real-time applications.
• Description:
The proposed system integrates AI/ML-driven noise suppression with adaptive filtering to create a robust ANC pipeline. The development begins with dataset generation, where clean speech data is combined with curated defence noise datasets (gunshots, drones, artillery, vehicle engines, wind, etc.)
at varying SNR levels. This synthetic data generation ensures coverage of both stationary and impulsive noise scenarios.
The training pipeline involves transforming audio into time-frequency representations (e.g., STFT spectrograms) or directly using raw waveform inputs. Models process both full-band and sub-band features to capture global and local dependencies. while its also operates in the complex domain to preserve phase information. Training is performed using loss functions such as SI-SNR, L1/L2 loss, and perceptual loss, with evaluation metrics including SNR, STOI, and PESQ. Data augmentation techniques (random noise mixing, reverberation, clipping) are applied to improve generalization.
During inference, the trained model processes incoming noisy audio in real time, estimating a mask or directly reconstructing enhanced speech. The system can optionally include a lightweight adaptive filter (e.g., LMS) for residual noise suppression.
For prototype demonstration, the trained model is deployed on embedded/edge hardware such as DSPs or AI-enabled SoCs (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB Developer Kit or similar platforms). Optimization techniques like quantization, pruning, and ONNX / TensorRT conversion are applied to meet latency and power constraints. The system is integrated with microphones (primary + reference) and headphones/communication units to validate real-time ANC performance in practical environments
• Expected Solution:
The final solution is a hybrid AI-driven ANC system capable of operating in real-time and handling diverse noise environments, including impulsive and highly dynamic defence scenarios. It should include:
• A scalable dataset pipeline for generating realistic noisy-clean speech pairs
• A state-of-the-art AI/ML model trained for robust noise suppression
• A training framework with optimized hyper-parameters and perceptual loss functions
• A real-time inference engine deployable on edge hardware
• A prototype system demonstrating live noise cancellation using microphones / headset integration The system is expected to achieve significant performance improvements, targeting SNR > 15 dB, STOI > 0.85, and PESQ > 2.5, while maintaining low latency suitable for real-time communication. This solution will enable reliable and intelligible communication in defence, aerospace, and high-noise industrial environments.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, artificial intelligence, ml applied to a smart vehicles problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (2/5): as a hardware build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Smart Vehicles. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on integration, model, real-time. Sustainability (2/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 19/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: AI/ML-Enabled Adaptive Noise Cancellation for Defence Communication

overview.in_plain_terms: Build an AI system that filters out gunfire, artillery, and vehicle noise from military radio communications in real time, so soldiers can actually understand each other during combat, while running on small embedded hardware, not a data center.
overview.why_it_matters: Garbled communication during combat has direct safety and mission consequences. Better noise cancellation isn't a convenience feature here, it's operational reliability.
pain_points: Traditional signal processing (spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering) fails against highly dynamic, non-stationary combat noise.
Existing methods introduce artifacts or distort speech under rapidly changing conditions.
Real-time performance on embedded hardware is required, not just offline processing.
overview.background: Defence communication systems face severe acoustic disruption from combat noise (gunfire, artillery, vehicles), and traditional signal processing techniques can't handle the highly dynamic, non-stationary nature of these disturbances effectively.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI/ML-based adaptive noise cancellation system suppressing stationary, non-stationary, and impulsive noise while preserving speech intelligibility, running in real time on embedded hardware.
expected_solution: Deep learning-based noise suppression outperforming traditional signal processing.
Handling of stationary, non-stationary, and impulsive (gunshot-type) noise specifically.
Preserved speech intelligibility (measurable via PESQ/STOI metrics).

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. AI-based speech enhancement is an active research area; the combination of handling impulsive combat-specific noise types plus genuine real-time embedded deployment is a real, hard engineering challenge.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires real audio ML expertise, dataset construction/sourcing for combat-type noise, model training, and embedded optimization, substantial technical depth across multiple specializations.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine audio ML and embedded systems expertise together, a narrower, more technical field than typical AI hackathon pitches.

innovation.note: AI-based ANC handling genuinely non-stationary, impulsive combat noise is real, active-research-adjacent technical territory.

invention.note: Requires audio ML modeling, realistic noise dataset construction, and embedded real-time optimization together.

technical_feasibility.note: Real combat-noise recordings aren't accessible; genuine embedded real-time deployment (not just a desktop demo) adds significant additional constraint.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly impacts communication reliability in life-safety-relevant combat scenarios.

architecture.note: Deep learning model plus real-time embedded deployment constraints together represent significant architectural difficulty.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Yellow. Genuinely technically substantial and valuable, but real embedded real-time deployment plus authentic combat-noise data are both hard constraints. A team should build and validate on desktop/simulated hardware with synthetic combat-noise data, and be explicit that true embedded real-time validation is a further step.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified technical evaluation criteria (PESQ, STOI, SNR metrics named explicitly), giving concrete, measurable success criteria rather than vague quality claims.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Claiming genuine real-time embedded performance without actually testing on embedded hardware (versus a desktop GPU) would be a meaningful overclaim, this constraint is explicitly named in the PS.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Decide upfront whether your team can genuinely test on embedded/edge hardware, or whether you'll build and validate on desktop first and be explicit that embedded deployment is the next validation step, not something you've confirmed.

idea_0_4: Source or construct a synthetic combat-noise dataset (mixing speech with recordings/simulations of gunfire, engine noise, sirens), real combat audio won't be accessible.
Choose your model architecture, lightweight time-domain models are more embedded-deployment-realistic than large spectral models.
Split: one person on model training/audio ML, one on embedded optimization/deployment testing.
prototype_4_22: Build your synthetic noise dataset with a mix of stationary, non-stationary, and impulsive noise types layered onto clean speech.
Train your noise-suppression model, prioritize a working baseline before optimizing.
Start measuring your model against the named metrics (PESQ, STOI) to have concrete evaluation numbers.
integration_22_30: Test your model's real-time inference speed, ideally on actual embedded/edge hardware if available, or at minimum on CPU-constrained conditions approximating it.
Compare your AI-based approach against a traditional method (spectral subtraction or Wiener filtering) on the same test noise, quantify the improvement.
Test specifically on impulsive noise (a sudden gunshot-type transient) since this is explicitly named as a traditional-method weakness.
polish_30_36: Prepare your PESQ/STOI comparison results (your model versus traditional method) as your key evidence.
Rehearse a live demo playing noisy audio through your system and the cleaned output, letting judges hear the difference directly.
Prepare to discuss the desktop-versus-embedded validation gap honestly if you weren't able to test on real embedded hardware.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Play a live audio comparison during the demo, noisy input with an impulsive gunshot-type sound layered in, versus your model's cleaned output, letting judges actually hear the difference is far more convincing than a metrics table alone.

strengths: Very well-specified, measurable success criteria (PESQ, STOI, SNR) give concrete evaluation targets.
Real, mission-critical impact case with clear technical stakes.
weaknesses: Real combat-noise data isn't accessible, synthetic data quality determines how convincing the demo is.
Genuine embedded real-time validation is a hard constraint that may not be fully achievable without real target hardware.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Audio ML-heavy, with a dedicated embedded-optimization role if genuine real-time hardware testing is attempted.
team_fit.approach: Build and validate on desktop first to get the model working, then attempt embedded optimization as a stretch goal, don't let embedded constraints block getting a working model at all.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard audio ML model architectures and training pipelines, well-documented patterns for speech enhancement.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Constructing a genuinely realistic synthetic combat-noise dataset (correct noise types, realistic mixing, appropriate SNR ranges) and correctly interpreting whether embedded real-time constraints are actually met, not just claimed.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A model that performs well on desktop but was never actually tested for real-time embedded feasibility could be presented as solving the PS when the genuinely hard embedded-deployment constraint remains unaddressed.

data_resource_availability.status: Real defence combat-noise recordings are not accessible to a hackathon team, this must be synthesized.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Construct a synthetic dataset mixing clean speech with publicly available noise recordings (gunfire sound effects, engine/vehicle noise, siren sounds) at varied, realistic SNR levels, clearly labeled as synthetic.

judge_qna.question: Did you actually test real-time performance on embedded hardware, or just on a desktop/laptop?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct about what you actually tested, if desktop-only, acknowledge that embedded real-time validation is the explicit next step, and discuss what model optimization (quantization, pruning) would be needed to get there.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your model's current inference latency, and what embedded hardware target would you need to hit for real deployment?

judge_qna.question: How realistic is your synthetic combat-noise dataset compared to actual field recordings?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be honest about the gap, real combat audio has characteristics (echo, distance, equipment-specific distortion) that synthetic mixing may not fully capture, describe what real-world data collection would add.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the biggest risk that your model overfits to your specific synthetic noise characteristics rather than generalizing to real combat audio?
